lesson.title: Comparing Two Groups: A Confidence Interval for the Difference in Proportions
lesson.summary: A confidence interval for p1 minus p2 estimates how far apart two population proportions really are, combining each group's own variability because the variance of a difference of independent quantities is the sum of their variances.
lesson.body:
Many real questions are not about a single proportion but about comparing two groups: do two treatments have different success rates, do two demographic groups differ in support for a policy, did a website redesign change the conversion rate compared to the old design. These questions call for a confidence interval built around the difference in two independent sample proportions, p-hat1 minus p-hat2.

The point estimate for the interval is simply p-hat1 minus p-hat2. The harder part is the standard error, and this is where the earlier idea of the difference of random variables becomes essential. For two independent random variables, the variance of their difference is the sum of their individual variances, not the difference of the variances, subtraction of the means still means addition of the variances, because independent sources of variability compound rather than cancel. Applying that fact to two independent sample proportions gives the standard error of the difference as the square root of p-hat1(1-p-hat1)/n1 plus p-hat2(1-p-hat2)/n2. The full interval is then (p-hat1 minus p-hat2) plus or minus z star times that standard error.

Worked example: a school district pilots two tutoring programs and tracks whether students pass an end-of-year exam. Program A had 250 students, 175 of whom passed, so p-hat1 = 175/250 = 0.70. Program B had 250 students, 150 of whom passed, so p-hat2 = 150/250 = 0.60. The point estimate for the difference is 0.70 minus 0.60 = 0.10. The standard error is the square root of (0.70 times 0.30 divided by 250) plus (0.60 times 0.40 divided by 250), which is the square root of 0.00084 plus 0.00096, or the square root of 0.0018, about 0.0424. At 95 percent confidence, z star is 1.96, so the margin of error is 1.96 times 0.0424, about 0.0832. The interval is therefore 0.10 minus 0.0832 to 0.10 plus 0.0832, or about 0.017 to 0.183.

Because this entire interval, roughly 1.7 percentage points to 18.3 percentage points, is above zero, the data suggest Program A's true pass rate is genuinely higher than Program B's, not just higher by chance in this particular pair of samples. Before trusting that conclusion, the same style of conditions used for a single proportion applies to each group separately: both samples need to be random or from randomized assignment, each sample should be no more than 10 percent of its respective population if sampled without replacement, and the Large Counts condition should hold in each group. Checking here, 250 times 0.70 = 175, 250 times 0.30 = 75, 250 times 0.60 = 150, and 250 times 0.40 = 100, all comfortably above 10, so the interval is trustworthy.
